content: COROS Intensity Trend (the load ratio) is Load Impact divided by Base Fitness. Load Impact is the 7-day average of daily training load; Base Fitness is the 42-day average. COROS shows it as a percentage and maps it to a status label. These are COROS's own model, not validated science.

COROS labels by load ratio: Decreasing below 50%, Resuming or Performance 50-79%, Maintaining 80-99%, Optimized 100-149%, Excessive 150% and above. Resuming and Performance share a band; the label depends on the previous status. Exact edge wording varies slightly between COROS pages.

COROS says an Excessive status (ratio 150% or more) points to recent load far above the long-term base and possible overreaching, and suggests easing load. It is a signal to check how you feel, not a diagnosis.

COROS describes Optimized (100-149%) as recent load that builds base fitness, and Maintaining (80-99%) as moderate recent load that keeps base fitness steady. Decreasing and Resuming mean recent load is below the base, so fitness may fall or is only starting to recover.

COROS weekly training load is the sum of workout loads from Monday to Sunday. It shows a suggested range learned from your own habits and gives no fixed numeric bounds, since what counts as low or high differs by person.

topic: Acute to chronic workload ratio sweet spot
content: Gabbett (2016) proposed keeping the acute to chronic workload ratio around 0.8-1.3, with 1.5 and above as a danger zone, and limiting weekly load rises. The evidence came mostly from team sports such as cricket and rugby, and the author cautions against applying it to one person.

Impellizzeri and colleagues (2020) argue there is no evidence that the acute to chronic workload ratio should guide load decisions to prevent injury, and that the ratio has statistical problems. So a ratio in a given band should not be presented as a proven injury predictor.

In a one-year study of 874 novice runners, those who raised weekly distance by over 30% did not have a significantly higher overall injury rate than those under 10%. Only a small, not statistically significant signal appeared for some distance-related injuries. The 10% rule is therefore weakly supported.

topic: Rapid load changes and injury risk
content: An IOC consensus statement (2016) says poor load management, including rapid changes in training load, is a major risk factor for injury and illness, and recommends monitoring load and changing it gradually.

Seiler (2010) observed that elite endurance athletes spend about 80% of sessions at low intensity and about 20% hard. This is a description of elites; supporting trials are small and short, so treat 80/20 as a common guideline, not a rule.

Reviews of tapering agree on the direction: before a key race, cut training volume but keep intensity, and reduce frequency only slightly. Well-planned tapers improved performance by about 3% on average.

Sources differ on how much to taper. One meta-analysis found best results with a two-week taper cutting volume by 41-60% progressively; an earlier review reported cuts up to 60-90% over 4 to 28+ days. Most samples were not pure runners.

A joint ECSS and ACSM consensus separates functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome, and says telling the last two apart is difficult and needs clinical assessment. A chatbot should not diagnose these; persistent fatigue or poor performance calls for a professional.

topic: Resting heart rate and HRV need a personal baseline
content: Reviews of heart-rate based monitoring say changes in resting heart rate or HRV should be read against your own baseline, normal day-to-day noise and training context. No universal cut-offs exist; both rises and falls can mean different things in different athletes.
